_link.title: I can identify the key differences between cancer cells and normal cells

toLevel2.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of cancer cells that distinguishes them from normal cells?

options.text: They divide without growth factor signals
options.explanation: Cancer cells do not need external growth factor signals to divide, unlike normal cells which require them.

options.text: They stop dividing when they contact neighbours
options.explanation: Normal cells stop dividing upon contact inhibition; cancer cells ignore this signal.

options.text: They divide a limited number of times only
options.explanation: Normal cells have a limited number of divisions; cancer cells can divide indefinitely.

options.text: They remain fixed at their site of origin
options.explanation: Cancer cells can metastasise and spread to new locations via the bloodstream.

options.text: The spread of cancer cells to new locations via the bloodstream
options.explanation: Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells travel through the blood or lymph to form secondary tumours.

options.text: The programmed death of damaged cells in the body
options.explanation: Programmed cell death is apoptosis, not metastasis.

options.text: The repair of damaged DNA during the cell cycle process
options.explanation: DNA repair is a checkpoint function, not metastasis.

options.text: The normal division of cells during the growth phase
options.explanation: Normal cell division is part of the cell cycle; metastasis is cancer spread.

toLevel2.question: What is angiogenesis in the context of cancer?

options.text: The growth of new blood vessels to supply a tumour
options.explanation: Cancer cells can trigger angiogenesis, stimulating new blood vessel growth to deliver nutrients to the tumour.

options.text: The destruction of blood vessels near a tumour
options.explanation: Angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels, not their destruction.

options.text: The process of cancer cells undergoing apoptosis
options.explanation: Apoptosis is programmed cell death; angiogenesis is new blood vessel growth.

options.text: The movement of white blood cells to a tumour
options.explanation: White blood cell movement is an immune response; angiogenesis is blood vessel formation.

toLevel2.question: How many times can a healthy normal cell typically divide before it stops?

options.text: About 50 times
options.explanation: Normal cells divide approximately 50 times before they wear out, a limit cancer cells do not have.

options.text: About 10 times
options.explanation: Normal cells can divide about 50 times, not 10.

options.text: An unlimited number of times
options.explanation: Unlimited division is a feature of cancer cells; normal cells divide about 50 times.

options.text: About 500 times
options.explanation: Normal cells divide about 50 times, not 500.

toLevel2.question: What structural feature is commonly observed in cancer cell nuclei?

options.text: They are darker and larger than normal
options.explanation: Cancer cells typically have darker, larger nuclei with disorganised chromosomes compared to normal cells.

options.text: They are smaller and lighter than normal
options.explanation: Cancer cell nuclei are characteristically darker and larger, not smaller and lighter.

options.text: They are identical to normal cell nuclei
options.explanation: Cancer cell nuclei differ from normal ones; they are larger, darker, and contain disorganised chromosomes.

options.text: They lack a nuclear membrane entirely
options.explanation: Cancer cells still have nuclei with membranes; the nuclei are larger and darker.

toLevel2.question: Cancer cells ignore contact inhibition and continue dividing even when surrounded by neighbouring cells.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Normal cells stop dividing when they contact neighbours, but cancer cells ignore this signal and keep dividing.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Cancer cells do not respond to contact inhibition, which is why they form disorganised tumours.

toLevel2.question: Normal cells can divide indefinitely without any limit on the number of divisions.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Normal cells divide about 50 times before they stop. It is cancer cells that can divide indefinitely.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. Normal cells have a limited number of divisions (about 50). Cancer cells, not normal cells, can divide indefinitely.

toLevel2.question: Cancer cells can {{blank:1}} to new locations in the body via the {{blank:2}}.

options.text: metastasise
options.explanation: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the original tumour to distant sites.

options.text: differentiate
options.explanation: Differentiation is when cells become specialised; metastasis is the spread of cancer.

options.text: regenerate
options.explanation: Regeneration is tissue repair; metastasis is cancer cell spread to new locations.

options.text: bloodstream
options.explanation: Cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system to form secondary tumours.

options.text: cell membrane
options.explanation: Cancer cells spread through the bloodstream, not through cell membranes.

options.text: nuclear pore
options.explanation: Nuclear pores are structures in the nucleus; cancer cells spread via the bloodstream.

toLevel2.question: Cancer cells divide without {{blank:1}} signals and can trigger {{blank:2}} to supply the tumour with nutrients.

options.text: growth factor
options.explanation: Normal cells require growth factor signals to divide; cancer cells do not.

options.text: nerve impulse
options.explanation: Cell division is regulated by growth factors, not nerve impulses.

options.text: hormone only
options.explanation: The key missing signal in cancer cells is growth factor signalling, not hormones.

options.text: angiogenesis
options.explanation: Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels that supply tumours with nutrients.

options.text: apoptosis
options.explanation: Apoptosis is programmed cell death; angiogenesis is new blood vessel growth.

options.text: osmosis
options.explanation: Osmosis is water movement across membranes; angiogenesis is blood vessel formation.

toLevel2.question: Structurally, cancer cells show variation in {{blank:1}} and shape, and have {{blank:2}} chromosomes.

options.text: size
options.explanation: Cancer cells show variation in size and shape, unlike the uniform appearance of normal cells.

options.text: colour
options.explanation: Cancer cells vary in size and shape; colour variation is not a defining structural feature.

options.text: number
options.explanation: The key structural variation in cancer cells is in their size and shape.

options.text: disorganised
options.explanation: Cancer cells have disorganised chromosomes, reflecting their loss of normal regulation.

options.text: missing
options.explanation: Cancer cells have chromosomes that are disorganised, not entirely missing.

options.text: duplicated
options.explanation: The key feature is disorganised chromosomes, not simply duplicated ones.

toLevel3.question: Why does the ability of cancer cells to ignore contact inhibition lead to tumour formation?

options.text: They continue dividing and pile up into disorganised masses instead of forming orderly layers
options.explanation: Normal cells form orderly tissue layers because they stop dividing on contact. Cancer cells ignore this and keep dividing, forming tumours.

options.text: They stop dividing too early and form gaps in the tissue structure
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide excessively, not too little; they pile up rather than leaving gaps.

options.text: They move away from each other and spread tissue layers too thinly
options.explanation: Cancer cells pile up into masses; they do not spread layers too thinly.

options.text: They form orderly layers that are thicker than normal tissue
options.explanation: Cancer cells form disorganised masses, not orderly layers.

toLevel3.question: Why is metastasis considered the most dangerous feature of malignant tumours?

options.text: It allows cancer to spread to distant organs and form secondary tumours throughout the body
options.explanation: Metastasis spreads cancer beyond the original site, making treatment harder and affecting multiple organs.

options.text: It causes the original tumour to shrink and disappear over time
options.explanation: Metastasis spreads cancer; it does not cause the original tumour to shrink.

options.text: It prevents the immune system from detecting the tumour
options.explanation: While immune evasion can occur, the danger of metastasis is specifically the spread to new sites.

options.text: It only affects the bloodstream and no other body systems
options.explanation: Metastasis uses the bloodstream to spread cancer to organs like lungs, liver, and brain.

toLevel3.question: How does angiogenesis benefit the growth of a tumour?

options.text: New blood vessels deliver oxygen and nutrients that sustain rapid tumour growth
options.explanation: Without a blood supply, tumours cannot grow beyond a small size. Angiogenesis provides the resources needed for continued growth.

options.text: New blood vessels carry cancer cells away from the tumour to destroy them
options.explanation: Angiogenesis supplies the tumour; while blood vessels can carry cancer cells, the primary benefit to the tumour is nutrient supply.

options.text: New blood vessels compress the tumour and limit its overall size
options.explanation: Angiogenesis supports tumour growth rather than limiting it.

options.text: New blood vessels replace the cancer cells with healthy tissue
options.explanation: Angiogenesis feeds the tumour; it does not replace cancer cells with healthy ones.

toLevel3.question: What is the key difference between a benign tumour and a malignant tumour?

options.text: Malignant tumours can metastasise while benign tumours remain at their original site
options.explanation: The ability to metastasise and spread to distant sites is what makes malignant tumours more dangerous than benign ones.

options.text: Benign tumours grow faster than malignant tumours in all cases
options.explanation: Malignant tumours often grow rapidly; the key difference is metastasis, not growth rate.

options.text: Malignant tumours are always smaller than benign tumours
options.explanation: Size does not determine malignancy; the key distinction is the ability to metastasise.

options.text: Benign tumours have disorganised chromosomes while malignant ones do not
options.explanation: Malignant cancer cells show disorganised chromosomes; benign tumours are less abnormal.

toLevel3.question: Why do cancer cells have darker, larger nuclei compared to normal cells?

options.text: They contain more DNA due to disorganised chromosomes and uncontrolled replication
options.explanation: The larger, darker nuclei reflect increased DNA content and chromosomal disorganisation from uncontrolled division.

options.text: They have lost all of their chromosomes through repeated division cycles
options.explanation: Cancer cells have disorganised chromosomes, not absent ones; their nuclei are larger due to excess DNA.

options.text: They produce more chlorophyll than normal human cell nuclei
options.explanation: Human cells do not produce chlorophyll; the darker staining is due to excess DNA content.

options.text: They are stained differently in the lab for identification purposes
options.explanation: The darker appearance reflects genuine structural differences, not just staining technique.

toLevel3.question: How does the division rate of cancer cells compare to that of normal cells, and why is this significant?

options.text: Cancer cells divide far more frequently, allowing tumours to grow rapidly
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide much more often than normal cells and have no division limit, enabling rapid tumour growth.

options.text: Cancer cells divide at the same rate but live longer than normal cells
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide more frequently than normal cells; the increased rate is a key characteristic.

options.text: Cancer cells divide less often but produce larger daughter cells
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide more frequently, not less; this rapid division drives tumour growth.

options.text: Cancer cells only divide once then stop permanently at that point
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide indefinitely; it is normal cells that have a limited number of divisions.

toLevel3.question: A benign tumour is less dangerous than a malignant tumour because benign tumours cannot metastasise to other parts of the body.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Benign tumours remain localised, while malignant tumours can metastasise and spread to distant organs.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. The inability to metastasise is a key reason benign tumours are less dangerous.

toLevel3.question: Normal cells form orderly tissue layers due to {{blank:1}}, whereas cancer cells ignore this and form {{blank:2}}.

options.text: contact inhibition
options.explanation: Contact inhibition causes normal cells to stop dividing when they touch neighbouring cells.

options.text: active transport
options.explanation: Active transport moves molecules across membranes; contact inhibition regulates cell division.

options.text: osmotic balance
options.explanation: Osmotic balance relates to water movement; contact inhibition controls cell division.

options.text: disorganised tumours
options.explanation: Without contact inhibition, cancer cells pile up into disorganised masses called tumours.

options.text: orderly tissue layers
options.explanation: Cancer cells form disorganised masses, not orderly layers; that is what normal cells do.

options.text: single-cell layers only
options.explanation: Cancer cells pile up into masses; they do not form single layers.

toLevel3.question: Malignant tumours are more dangerous than {{blank:1}} tumours because malignant cells can {{blank:2}} to distant organs.

options.text: benign
options.explanation: Benign tumours remain localised and cannot spread, unlike malignant tumours.

options.text: normal
options.explanation: The correct comparison is between malignant and benign tumours, not normal tissue.

options.text: healthy
options.explanation: The medical term for non-spreading tumours is benign, not healthy.

options.text: metastasise
options.explanation: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the primary tumour to distant body sites.

options.text: differentiate
options.explanation: Differentiation is becoming specialised; metastasis is the spread of cancer cells.

options.text: regenerate
options.explanation: Regeneration is tissue repair; metastasis is cancer cell spread to new locations.

toLevel3.question: Cancer cells divide {{blank:1}} compared to normal cells and can divide {{blank:2}}, unlike normal cells which stop after about 50 divisions.

options.text: more frequently
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide far more often than normal cells, contributing to rapid tumour growth.

options.text: less frequently
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide more frequently than normal cells, not less.

options.text: at the same rate
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide much more frequently than normal cells.

options.text: indefinitely
options.explanation: Cancer cells have no limit on divisions, while normal cells stop after about 50.

options.text: only once
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide indefinitely, not just once.

options.text: exactly 50 times
options.explanation: About 50 divisions is the limit for normal cells; cancer cells divide indefinitely.

toLevel4.question: A tissue sample shows cells with large, dark nuclei, variable sizes, and disorganised chromosomes. What would a pathologist most likely conclude?

options.text: The sample contains cancerous cells based on the structural abnormalities
options.explanation: Large dark nuclei, variable cell sizes, and disorganised chromosomes are hallmark structural features of cancer cells.

options.text: The sample contains normal cells undergoing standard mitosis
options.explanation: Normal cells in mitosis maintain uniform size and organised chromosomes.

options.text: The sample contains stem cells that are differentiating normally
options.explanation: Differentiating stem cells do not show the nuclear and chromosomal abnormalities described.

options.text: The sample contains dead cells undergoing necrosis in the tissue
options.explanation: Necrosis shows cell swelling and lysis, not the large dark nuclei characteristic of cancer.

toLevel4.question: A researcher discovers that a new drug blocks angiogenesis. Predict how this drug could affect tumour growth.

options.text: The tumour would be starved of nutrients and oxygen, limiting its growth
options.explanation: Without new blood vessels, the tumour cannot receive the oxygen and nutrients needed for continued growth.

options.text: The tumour would grow faster because blood flow is redirected to it
options.explanation: Blocking angiogenesis reduces blood supply to the tumour, not increases it.

options.text: The tumour cells would immediately undergo normal cell division
options.explanation: Blocking angiogenesis starves the tumour but does not restore normal cell cycle control.

options.text: The drug would have no effect on the tumour growth at all
options.explanation: Tumours depend on angiogenesis for growth; blocking it would restrict their nutrient supply.

toLevel4.question: A patient is diagnosed with a tumour that has not spread beyond its original site. Based on the characteristics of cancer, what type of tumour is this?

options.text: A benign tumour, because it has not metastasised
options.explanation: Benign tumours remain at their original site and do not metastasise to other locations.

options.text: A malignant tumour, because all tumours are malignant
options.explanation: Not all tumours are malignant; benign tumours stay localised and do not metastasise.

options.text: A secondary tumour from metastasis at that particular site
options.explanation: A secondary tumour results from metastasis; this tumour has not spread.

options.text: A normal growth that requires no medical attention at all
options.explanation: Even benign tumours may require monitoring; the lack of spread indicates benign status.

toLevel4.question: In a cell culture experiment, normal cells stop dividing when they form a single layer, but a second cell line keeps dividing and piles up. What can you conclude about the second cell line?

options.text: The second cell line has lost contact inhibition, a feature of cancer cells
options.explanation: Loss of contact inhibition causes cells to ignore neighbours and continue dividing, a hallmark of cancer.

options.text: The second cell line is healthier and grows better than normal cells
options.explanation: Ignoring contact inhibition is not a sign of health; it is a cancer cell characteristic.

options.text: The second cell line has stronger contact inhibition than the first line
options.explanation: Stronger contact inhibition would cause cells to stop dividing sooner, not pile up.

options.text: The second cell line is undergoing normal apoptosis in the culture
options.explanation: Apoptosis is cell death; the piling up indicates continued division, not death.

toLevel4.question: A scientist finds that cancer cells from a lung tumour have appeared in the patient's liver. Which cancer cell characteristic explains this finding?

options.text: Metastasis allowed the cancer cells to spread via the bloodstream to the liver
options.explanation: Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells travel through blood or lymph to establish secondary tumours in distant organs.

options.text: Angiogenesis caused the liver to produce its own cancer cells independently
options.explanation: Angiogenesis is blood vessel growth; the liver cancer originated from lung cancer cells that metastasised.

options.text: Contact inhibition caused the lung cancer cells to move to the liver
options.explanation: Contact inhibition is about stopping division; metastasis explains the spread to the liver.

options.text: The liver cells spontaneously transformed into lung cancer cells
options.explanation: The cancer cells spread from the lung via metastasis; liver cells did not transform.

toLevel4.question: A drug is designed to restore contact inhibition in cancer cells. Predict the effect of this drug on tumour growth.

options.text: Cancer cells would stop dividing when they contact neighbours, slowing tumour growth
options.explanation: Restoring contact inhibition would cause cancer cells to behave more like normal cells and stop dividing when crowded.

options.text: Cancer cells would divide even faster than before the drug was applied
options.explanation: Restoring contact inhibition slows division; it does not accelerate it.

options.text: The tumour would immediately metastasise to all organs throughout the body
options.explanation: Restoring contact inhibition limits division; it does not trigger metastasis.

options.text: The drug would have no effect because contact inhibition is irrelevant
options.explanation: Loss of contact inhibition is a key cancer feature; restoring it would limit tumour growth.

toLevel4.question: A patient's biopsy shows cells that divide without growth factor signals and have triggered new blood vessel formation. What do these features together indicate?

options.text: The cells are cancerous, showing growth factor independence and angiogenesis
options.explanation: Both dividing without growth factors and triggering angiogenesis are hallmark cancer cell behaviours.

options.text: The cells are normal and undergoing standard wound healing processes
options.explanation: Normal wound healing requires growth factor signals; independence from them indicates cancer.

options.text: The cells are stem cells that are differentiating into blood vessels
options.explanation: Stem cell differentiation does not involve growth factor independence; these features indicate cancer.

options.text: The cells are dead and cannot divide or trigger any growth response
options.explanation: The cells are actively dividing and triggering angiogenesis, indicating they are alive and cancerous.

toLevel4.question: In a cell culture, normal cells stop dividing at a single layer due to {{blank:1}}, but cancer cells continue to {{blank:2}} and form masses.

options.text: contact inhibition
options.explanation: Contact inhibition stops normal cells from dividing when they touch neighbouring cells.

options.text: active transport
options.explanation: Active transport moves molecules; contact inhibition regulates cell division.

options.text: binary fission
options.explanation: Binary fission is prokaryotic division; contact inhibition stops eukaryotic cell division.

options.text: divide and pile up
options.explanation: Cancer cells ignore contact inhibition and keep dividing, piling up into disorganised masses.

options.text: shrink and die
options.explanation: Cancer cells continue growing; they do not shrink and die when crowded.

options.text: stop and repair
options.explanation: Cancer cells do not stop; they continue dividing, which is the hallmark abnormality.

toLevel4.question: Blocking {{blank:1}} would starve a tumour of {{blank:2}} and oxygen, limiting its growth.

options.text: angiogenesis
options.explanation: Blocking angiogenesis prevents new blood vessel growth, cutting off the tumour's supply.

options.text: metastasis
options.explanation: Blocking metastasis stops spread, but angiogenesis is what delivers nutrients to the tumour.

options.text: apoptosis
options.explanation: Blocking apoptosis would prevent cell death; blocking angiogenesis starves the tumour.

options.text: nutrients
options.explanation: Blood vessels deliver nutrients and oxygen; blocking their formation starves the tumour.

options.text: chromosomes
options.explanation: Chromosomes are inside cells; blood vessels deliver nutrients and oxygen to the tumour.

options.text: nerve signals
options.explanation: Tumour growth depends on nutrients from blood vessels, not nerve signals.

toLevel4.question: When lung cancer cells are found in the liver, this is evidence of {{blank:1}}, where cells travelled through the {{blank:2}}.

options.text: metastasis
options.explanation: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the primary site to distant organs.

options.text: angiogenesis
options.explanation: Angiogenesis is new blood vessel growth; metastasis is the spread of cancer to new sites.

options.text: differentiation
options.explanation: Differentiation is cells becoming specialised; metastasis is cancer spread.

options.text: bloodstream
options.explanation: Cancer cells metastasise by travelling through the bloodstream or lymphatic system.

options.text: cell membrane
options.explanation: Cancer cells travel through the bloodstream to reach distant organs.

options.text: nuclear pore
options.explanation: Nuclear pores are inside cells; cancer cells spread via the bloodstream.

toLevel5.question: A researcher compares two tumour samples. Tumour A has triggered extensive angiogenesis while Tumour B has not. Which tumour is more likely to grow rapidly, and why?

options.text: Tumour A, because angiogenesis provides the blood supply needed for sustained rapid growth
options.explanation: Angiogenesis delivers oxygen and nutrients; without it, Tumour B would be limited in size and growth rate.

options.text: Tumour B, because the absence of blood vessels forces faster cell division
options.explanation: Without blood vessels, cells lack nutrients; this limits growth rather than accelerating it.

options.text: Both tumours would grow at the same rate regardless of blood supply
options.explanation: Blood supply directly affects growth; angiogenesis gives Tumour A a growth advantage.

options.text: Tumour B, because blood vessels compress tumour tissue and slow growth
options.explanation: Blood vessels supply nutrients; they do not compress and slow tumour growth.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why targeting a single cancer characteristic, such as blocking angiogenesis alone, may not be sufficient to cure cancer.

options.text: Cancer cells have multiple abnormal features, so blocking one still leaves others like metastasis and uncontrolled division active
options.explanation: Cancer involves many simultaneous abnormalities; addressing only one leaves other dangerous characteristics unchecked.

options.text: Blocking angiogenesis would cure cancer completely because it is the only important feature
options.explanation: Angiogenesis is just one of many cancer characteristics; cells can still divide and metastasise.

options.text: Cancer cells only have one abnormal characteristic so targeting it cures the disease
options.explanation: Cancer cells have multiple abnormalities including uncontrolled division, metastasis, and growth factor independence.

options.text: Angiogenesis has no relevance to tumour growth or survival in the body
options.explanation: Angiogenesis is important for tumour growth, but it is not the only factor; multiple features contribute.

toLevel5.question: Compare the danger posed by a large benign tumour and a small malignant tumour. Which is potentially more dangerous?

options.text: The small malignant tumour, because it can metastasise and spread to vital organs
options.explanation: Metastasis makes malignant tumours dangerous regardless of size; benign tumours cannot spread to other organs.

options.text: The large benign tumour, because larger size always means greater danger
options.explanation: Size alone does not determine danger; the ability to metastasise makes malignant tumours more threatening.

options.text: Both pose exactly the same level of danger to the patient overall
options.explanation: Malignant tumours are more dangerous because they can metastasise; benign ones remain localised.

options.text: Neither is dangerous because all tumours are harmless to patients
options.explanation: Malignant tumours are dangerous due to metastasis; even benign tumours can cause problems by pressing on organs.

toLevel5.question: A scientist observes that cancer cells in a culture continue dividing even when growth factors are removed from the medium. Analyse what this reveals about the cells' signalling pathways.

options.text: Their growth signalling pathways are constitutively active and no longer depend on external signals
options.explanation: Cancer cells often have mutations that keep growth pathways permanently switched on, making external growth factors unnecessary.

options.text: They require growth factors but obtain them from the culture dish material itself
options.explanation: The observation shows independence from growth factors, not an alternative source of them.

options.text: Their signalling pathways have shut down entirely and cells divide by default
options.explanation: Division requires active signalling; in cancer, these pathways are constitutively active rather than shut down.

options.text: Removing growth factors has stimulated a dormancy response in the cancer cells
options.explanation: The cells continue dividing, not entering dormancy; their internal pathways are permanently activated.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the structural characteristics of cancer cells, such as variable size and disorganised chromosomes, are both a consequence and a cause of uncontrolled division.

options.text: Uncontrolled division causes chromosomal errors, and these errors further disrupt cell cycle regulation
options.explanation: Rapid, unregulated division leads to DNA replication errors and chromosomal disorganisation, which in turn further impairs regulatory mechanisms.

options.text: The structural changes are cosmetic and have no functional effect on cell behaviour
options.explanation: Structural abnormalities reflect and cause functional defects in cell cycle control.

options.text: Disorganised chromosomes always correct themselves during the next cell division
options.explanation: Without proper regulation, chromosomal disorganisation tends to worsen with each division.

options.text: Variable cell size prevents cancer cells from dividing any further
options.explanation: Variable size is a consequence of uncontrolled division; it does not prevent further division.

toLevel5.question: A patient has a malignant tumour that has metastasised to three different organs. Analyse why this makes treatment significantly more difficult than treating a single localised tumour.

options.text: Treatment must target cancer in multiple locations, and each site may respond differently to therapy
options.explanation: Metastatic cancer requires systemic treatment, and secondary tumours may have different characteristics from the primary tumour.

options.text: Metastatic tumours are always smaller and therefore harder to detect than primary tumours
options.explanation: Difficulty is not primarily about size; it is about treating multiple sites with potentially different characteristics.

options.text: Treatment is simpler because the same drug works equally well at all tumour sites
options.explanation: Metastatic tumours can develop different mutations, making uniform treatment less effective.

options.text: Metastasis has no impact on treatment because only the primary tumour matters
options.explanation: Secondary tumours are often what cause serious harm; treating only the primary site is insufficient.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why cancer cells that have both lost contact inhibition and gained the ability to trigger angiogenesis are particularly dangerous.

options.text: They can grow without spatial limits and sustain that growth with a dedicated blood supply
options.explanation: Loss of contact inhibition removes growth limits, while angiogenesis provides the resources for continued, unlimited growth.

options.text: Contact inhibition and angiogenesis are unrelated features that do not interact with each other
options.explanation: These features work together: unlimited division creates demand for nutrients that angiogenesis supplies.

options.text: Angiogenesis counteracts the loss of contact inhibition and slows tumour growth down
options.explanation: Angiogenesis supports tumour growth by providing nutrients; it does not counteract uncontrolled division.

options.text: Loss of contact inhibition prevents angiogenesis from occurring in the tumour at all
options.explanation: Both features can occur simultaneously, making the tumour more dangerous.

toLevel5.question: Compare the division characteristics of normal cells and cancer cells, and analyse which difference has the greatest impact on tumour development.

options.text: The loss of division limits is most impactful, as indefinite division enables continuous tumour growth
options.explanation: Normal cells stop after about 50 divisions; cancer cells dividing indefinitely allows tumours to grow without limit.

options.text: Normal and cancer cells divide at exactly the same rate with no key differences
options.explanation: Cancer cells divide more frequently and indefinitely, which are critical differences.

options.text: The size of daughter cells is the most important difference between the two types
options.explanation: While cell size varies in cancer, the loss of division limits is the most significant factor for tumour growth.

options.text: Normal cells divide faster than cancer cells under all conditions studied
options.explanation: Cancer cells typically divide faster and without limit, unlike normal cells.

toLevel5.question: Cancer is difficult to treat when cells have metastasised because the disease is no longer {{blank:1}} and may require {{blank:2}} treatment.

options.text: localised
options.explanation: Metastasis spreads cancer beyond the original site, making it no longer confined to one location.

options.text: visible
options.explanation: The key issue is that cancer is no longer in one place, not that it is invisible.

options.text: dividing
options.explanation: Cancer cells are still dividing; the issue is that they have spread to multiple locations.

options.text: systemic
options.explanation: Systemic treatment (e.g. chemotherapy) is needed because cancer has spread throughout the body.

options.text: surgical
options.explanation: Surgery targets localised tumours; metastatic cancer often requires systemic approaches.

options.text: topical
options.explanation: Topical treatment is for surface conditions; systemic treatment targets cancer throughout the body.

toLevel5.question: The combination of growth factor {{blank:1}} and the ability to trigger {{blank:2}} makes cancer cells capable of sustained, unlimited growth.

options.text: independence
options.explanation: Cancer cells do not need external growth factors; their signalling pathways are constitutively active.

options.text: dependence
options.explanation: Cancer cells are independent of growth factors, not dependent on them.

options.text: sensitivity
options.explanation: Cancer cells have lost sensitivity to growth factor requirements; they are independent.

options.text: angiogenesis
options.explanation: Angiogenesis provides the blood supply that fuels sustained tumour growth.

options.text: apoptosis
options.explanation: Apoptosis is cell death; angiogenesis is new blood vessel growth that supplies tumours.

options.text: osmosis
options.explanation: Osmosis is passive water movement; angiogenesis provides blood supply to tumours.
